guide.p: Education questions are extremely common: the purpose of school, university fees, online learning, exams, practical versus academic subjects. These words help you describe systems and arguments precisely.

bullets: Learn words in phrases, not alone: notice which verbs, adjectives and prepositions go with them.
Practise each word in a sentence about your own life or country — it will be easier to use in Speaking.
In Writing, choose the precise word over the impressive-sounding one. Accuracy beats complexity.

guide.tip: Be careful with 'learn' and 'teach': students learn, teachers teach. 'Study' is used for formal learning: 'I study economics.'

vocab.meaning: the subjects and content taught in a school or course
vocab.example: Coding has been added to the primary school curriculum.

vocab.meaning: required by law or rules
vocab.example: Education is compulsory until the age of sixteen.

vocab.meaning: money paid for teaching at a college or university
vocab.example: Tuition fees have tripled over the past decade.

vocab.meaning: education at college or university level
vocab.example: More young people are entering higher education than ever before.

vocab.meaning: relating to skills needed for a particular job
vocab.example: Vocational courses train students as electricians and chefs.

vocab.meaning: activities outside the normal timetable
vocab.example: Extracurricular activities such as sport and drama build confidence.

vocab.meaning: learning by repetition rather than understanding
vocab.example: Rote learning may help students pass exams but not solve problems.

vocab.meaning: the ability to analyse and judge information carefully
vocab.example: Universities value critical thinking above memory.

vocab.meaning: the process of judging students' work or ability
vocab.example: Continuous assessment reduces exam stress.

vocab.meaning: how well a student does in their studies
vocab.example: Sleep has a strong effect on academic performance.

vocab.meaning: the ability to read and write
vocab.example: Adult literacy rates have risen sharply.

vocab.meaning: the ability to use numbers
vocab.example: Basic numeracy is essential in everyday life.

vocab.meaning: money given to a student to pay for their studies
vocab.example: She won a scholarship to study medicine.

vocab.meaning: studying from home using online or posted materials
vocab.example: Distance learning suits people with full-time jobs.

vocab.meaning: a class with students of different levels
vocab.example: Teaching a mixed-ability class requires careful planning.

vocab.meaning: to leave a course before finishing it
vocab.example: Some students drop out because of financial pressure.

vocab.meaning: to complete a degree; a person who has done so
vocab.example: Graduates often struggle to find their first job.

vocab.meaning: a university student studying for a first degree
vocab.example: Undergraduates usually study for three or four years.

vocab.meaning: control of behaviour; also an academic subject
vocab.example: Strict discipline was common in schools in the past.

vocab.meaning: continuing to learn throughout life
vocab.example: Lifelong learning helps workers adapt to new technology.

vocab.meaning: work done during a course that counts towards the final grade
vocab.example: Coursework accounts for 40% of the final mark.

vocab.meaning: to focus on one particular subject
vocab.example: She decided to specialise in environmental law.

vocab.meaning: influence from people of the same age to behave in a certain way
vocab.example: Peer pressure can affect students' choices.

vocab.meaning: to gain abilities through learning or experience
vocab.example: Volunteering is a good way to acquire practical skills.
